# Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget

Hongyu Wu

Mike Wiegers Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA

Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design’s rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of _n_ designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30_/n_ for large _n_, compared with 2_/n_ for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

### 1 Introduction

Many design and operational decisions require a choice from a large finite set of designs whose performance is estimated through expensive simulation. Ordinal optimization (OO) addresses such problems by accepting good-enough designs and comparing their order rather than their values [1, 2]. OO measures selection success by the alignment probability, the probability that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good-enough designs. This required number is called the alignment level [3]. In constrained OO, a selected design needs to be feasible. Constrained OO has been applied to stochastic security-constrained unit commitment with high wind penetration, where a feasibility model guides a blind pick (sampling<tbc>

<tbc>designs uniformly at random without comparing their performance) among candidate schedules [4]. Recent studies continue to apply OO to stochastic job-shop scheduling [5], emergency- department resource allocation [6], and task scheduling in wireless edge computing [7].

Quantum minimum finding shows that coherent access can reduce the number of queries needed for selection [8]. A coherent comparison acts on a superposition of design pairs, and the resulting amplitudes can interfere before measurement. An algorithm can use this interference to favor better ranks in its output distribution. For OO, the question is whether this capability improves alignment probability at a fixed comparison budget and how any improvement depends on the size of the good-enough set. However, accepting more designs as good enough also makes classical selection easier. Assessing a quantum benefit therefore requires comparison with the classical optimum for the same target and comparison budget.

Asymptotic query bounds for quantum selection [8, 9] do not determine the exact alignment probability at a small, fixed comparison budget. Fixed-budget quantum simulation optimization has also been studied through convergence rates for the expected optimality gap under quantum simulation access [10]. That criterion measures loss in performance value, whereas alignment measures whether the selected rank meets the target. To the best of our knowledge, prior work has not determined the exact alignment optimum over all admissible classical or quantum strategies in the comparison model. This optimum is needed to distinguish a benefit of coherent access from a weakness of a particular classical selection rule.

To address this gap, we formulate quantum ordinal optimization (QOO) as a class of problems that maximize the worst-case alignment probability under a specified oracle model and query budget. The oracle, selected-set size and alignment level are part of the problem specification. As a first instance, we study exact coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design and alignment level one. Exact comparisons separate selection from estimation error, while a single output reduces alignment to meeting the rank target. For each budget and good-enough set, the objective is the largest alignment probability that can be guaranteed for every strict order of the designs. The budget counts only comparison queries. Estimation error and implementation cost require further models, as discussed in Section 8.

In this comparison problem, we establish the classical optimum for every budget smaller than the number of designs and determine the one-comparison quantum optimum. One comparison is the smallest budget at which selection can depend on the unknown order, yet it already permits a quantum gain. We report each value as an equivalent blind-pick size, the number of designs that a blind pick would need to reach the same alignment probability, which need not be an integer. Our main results are as follows.

1. For every good-enough set and every budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that the optimal alignment probability with exact classical comparisons equals that of a blind pick whose size exceeds the budget by one. A knockout among the blindly picked designs attains this probability. Although the comparisons can involve twice as many designs as their number, no adaptive procedure that returns one design does better than this blind pick when comparisons are exact.<tbc>

2. Averaged over a random order, the law of the rank of the design selected by a quantum algorithm is a polynomial in the rank. Its degree is at most twice the comparison budget or one less than the number of designs, whichever is smaller, and this bound is attained. By contrast, the degree for classical algorithms is at most the comparison budget. At one comparison the larger quantum degree is necessary for any gain.<tbc>

3. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set, with a matching upper certificate and an attaining algorithm. The value is affine in the smallest positive root of an explicit cubic, with closed forms for the best design and for the top half, and it gives the limiting success probability for a fixed good-enough fraction.<tbc>

4. For selecting the best design, the equivalent blind-pick size of one quantum comparison increases with the number of designs toward \((3+\sqrt{13})/2\approx 3.30\), compared with 2 for one classical comparison, and it exceeds that of two classical comparisons exactly when there are more than nine designs. For the top 5 percent of 1000 designs it is about 3.27. In the cases computed it decreases as the good-enough set grows, and for the top half of 1000 designs it is below that of two classical comparisons.

The one-comparison result also raises the question of how the quantum benefit changes as more comparisons are allowed. Known search bounds and the reduction in Section 8.1 show that for selecting the best design the quantum equivalent blind-pick size grows at most quadratically in the comparison budget [11, 12], and minimum finding attains this order when the number of designs is at least of the order of the square of the budget [8]. The classical size is the budget plus one, so the ratio of quantum to classical sizes grows at most in proportion to the budget and reaches that order when the designs are numerous enough. This paper determines the ratio exactly for one comparison.

Section 2 reviews related work, and Section 3 defines the model and measures. Sections 4- 6 establish the classical optimum, the quantum degree bound and the exact one-comparison value. Section 7 compares the values in OO terms, Section 8 discusses larger budgets, evaluations and computational cost, and Section 9 summarizes the findings.

## 2 Relation to prior work

The relevant literature treats selection from performance estimates, selection through comparisons and exact optimization of quantum query algorithms. We distinguish these settings because their oracles and success criteria determine which guarantees can be compared with OO alignment.

### Classical ordinal optimization.

OO uses the fact that an estimated order can converge faster than estimated values. For several common performance measures, the order converges exponentially fast in the simulation length [13]. Its selection rules include blind pick, which selects designs at random; the horse race, which selects the designs that look best under a crude model [3]; and budget allocation rules such as optimal computing budget allocation (OCBA) [14]. These rules are catalogued and compared in [2].

Classical OO compares selection rules mainly by simulation. Lau and Ho listed round-robin and pairwise comparison rules as yet to be studied [3]. These rules were later defined for noisy observations and compared numerically, and no universally best selection rule is known [2]. Apart from budget allocation rules such as OCBA, existing OO optimality results apply to the final selection given the observations. Under independent, identically distributed noise and equal allocation, choosing the observed top designs is optimal [2], and with design-dependent<tbc>

<tbc>noise the optimal rule ranks designs by their probability of being good enough [15]. These results do not optimize which comparisons to make.

### Quantum selection from estimated values.

For quantum best-arm identification with reward gaps \(\Delta_i\), order \(\sqrt{\sum_i\Delta_i^{-2}}\) queries suffice and are necessary, up to polylogarithmic factors [16]. Weaker oracle models change the rate [17]. Whether a speedup exists depends on access to the simulator’s randomness [18]. With a weak quantum oracle, a fixed-confidence algorithm identifies a given number of best arms as a set [19]. Quantum Grover adaptive search for discrete simulation optimization returns an \(\epsilon\)-optimal design with probability at least \(1-\delta\) using \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) queries for constant \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) [9]. That is a fixed-confidence guarantee. Hu and Hu study fixed-budget simulation optimization through the minimax expected optimality gap and establish convergence rates under quantum simulation access [10]. Both formulations use performance values estimated from a simulator. Here success depends only on the selected rank, and we determine exact finite-budget values in a comparison-oracle model.

### Selection with comparisons.

Minimum finding uses order \(\sqrt{n}\) comparisons against a moving threshold [8], and finding the _r_ smallest values needs order \(\sqrt{rn}\) for \(r\le n/2\) [20]. Bounds for approximating an order statistic give order \(\sqrt{n/r}\), up to logarithmic factors, for an output among the top _r_ [21]. Grover adaptive search has been analyzed for reaching one of the best _r_ points [22]. That work bounds the expected cost and computes the success probability numerically as a function of the number of function evaluations for two given algorithms. Comparison oracles on permutations are the standard setting of quantum lower bounds for sorting and element distinctness [23]. Wang and Ying use a bounded-error version of this comparison oracle [24].

### Exact results with few queries.

Grover’s algorithm is exactly optimal for search with one marked item [11]. Zero-error few-query algorithms for ordered search were found numerically [25, 26], and translation-invariant algorithms are optimal for that problem [27]. For small Boolean functions, optimal success probabilities have been computed numerically by semidefinite programming in a study of zero-error quantum query complexity [28], and optimal values are known for oracle problems with a group structure [29] and for one-query AND and EQUALITY [30]. Several of these results use the semidefinite characterization of quantum query algorithms [31].

The comparison results provide query bounds for selection, while the few-query results provide methods for optimizing success at a specified budget. Below, we formulate rank alignment under comparison access, establish the exact classical benchmark and apply these methods to the one-comparison quantum problem. Selection from estimated values requires a different evaluation model, as discussed in Section 8.2.

## 3 Model and performance measures

Determining the best alignment probability at a fixed budget requires a QOO problem to specify what information queries provide and what counts as a successful selection. We first define the problem class with these choices left to each problem. We then specialize it to exact comparisons with one selected design, for which the following sections establish the results.

## 3.1 Quantum ordinal optimization

**Definition 1** (Quantum ordinal optimization)**.** A quantum ordinal optimization problem specifies a class of unknown configurations, each of which determines a strict order of _n_ designs and may contain further data such as performance values or gaps. It specifies the good-enough set of the _r_ best designs, an oracle whose responses depend on the configuration, a budget of at most _q_ calls on every branch of an algorithm’s measurements and private randomness, and the size of the selected set and its alignment level. The oracle model specifies its quantum action and the response to a classical query. An algorithm succeeds when its output set contains at least the prescribed alignment level of good-enough designs.

An admissible quantum algorithm uses input-independent state preparation, unitary operations, measurements, private randomness and finite workspace. It has no postselection and no access to the configuration except through the specified oracle. The classical counterpart uses private randomness and adaptive queries to the same oracle on one classical input at a time. Both obey the prescribed query budget and selected-set size. The quantum value is the supremum, over admissible quantum algorithms, of the infimum of their success probabilities over the configuration class. The classical value is defined in the same way over classical algorithms.

The oracle can provide comparisons, evaluations or membership information, and the selected set can contain one or several designs. Each choice specifies a QOO problem with its own classical benchmark. For a fixed oracle and selected-set size, the quantum value of a QOO problem is the optimal success probability of a query problem at a fixed number of queries, the quantity studied for other problems in the few-query work of Section 2. What OO adds is the good-enough target with its alignment level, the size of the selected set, and the comparison with the optimal classical procedure and with blind pick. Section 8.2 discusses how changes in evaluation and selection affect the formulation.

## 3.2 The exact-comparison instance

We study the instance of Definition 1 whose configurations are all strict orders, with the exact comparison oracle, selected-set size one and alignment level one. Classical and quantum procedures use the same comparison rule and good-enough target. They differ in how they query that rule, and this instance requires neither performance values nor numerical gaps between designs.

Let [_n_]={1_,...,n_} label _n_ designs. Their unknown performance order is a strict order, encoded by the rank vector _x_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_), a permutation of [_n_] in which rank 1 is best. An algorithm receives labels and oracle answers, never ranks. For \(0\le r\le n\) the good-enough set is the true top _r_, \(G_r(x)=\{i:x_i\le r\}\). The algorithm outputs one label _I_, and it succeeds when \(I\in G_r(x)\). In OO terms the selected set is {_I_}, of size one, the alignment level is one, and the alignment probability is \(Pr[x_I\le r]\) [3]. For _r_=1, this is the probability of correct selection (PCS) in ranking and selection [32]. For _r\>_1, it is a rank-based form of the probability of good selection (PGS), where goodness requires rank at most _r_, whereas Eckman and Henderson define good selection by a mean performance gap from the best that is smaller than a prescribed tolerance [33].

### Comparison oracle.

A quantum comparison is the oracle

\(O_x|i,j,c,w\rangle=|i,j,c\oplus\mathbf{1}_{\{x_i<x_j\}},w\rangle,i,j\in[n],\) (1)

where _c_ is a response bit, _w_ is workspace, and **1**<sub>{_x<sub>i</sub>\<x<sub>i</sub>_}</sub>=0. This is the standard comparison oracle on permutations \[23, 24\]. A classical comparison queries one pair and receives the bit **1**<sub>{_x<sub>i</sub>\<x<sub>j</sub>_}</sub>. An admissible quantum algorithm in this instance obeys Definition 1, makes at most _q_ calls to (1) on every branch and outputs one label. Its only access to _x_ is through this oracle. A classical algorithm is an adaptive comparison tree with private randomness and at most _q_ comparisons on every branch. Only oracle calls are charged.

_Remark_ 1. A self-address _i=j_ returns no information about _x_. It is allowed for convenience, and no value in this paper depends on it, because every call already acts as the identity on the \(|+\rangle\) eigenspace of the response bit.

**Definition 2.** For \(q\ge 0\), \(n\ge 1\) and \(0\le r\le n\), the quantum value is

\(Q_q(n,r)=sup_Amin_xPr_x^A[x_I\le r],\) (2)

where _A_ ranges over admissible algorithms with budget _q_ and _x_ over strict orders. The classical value _C<sub>q</sub>(n,r_) is defined in the same way over classical algorithms.

## 3.3 Worst case and average case

The worst-case objective can be analyzed through a uniform random order because an algorithm may randomly relabel designs before making comparisons. The same relabeling is used throughout the run, so the comparison answers remain consistent.

**Proposition 1.** _For every admissible algorithm A there is an admissible algorithm_ \(A'\) _with the same budget whose success on every order equals the success of A averaged over a uniformly random order, and whose whole rank law has the same property. Consequently Q<sub>q</sub>(n,r_) _and C<sub>q</sub>(n,r_) _equal the suprema of the uniform-average success._

_Proof._ Let \(A'\) draw a uniform permutation \(\sigma\) of \[_n_\] from private randomness, and let

\(P_\sigma|i,j,c,w\rangle=|\sigma(i),\sigma(j),c,w\rangle.\)

Then \(P_\sigma^{-1}O_xP_\sigma=O_{x\circ\sigma}\), where \((x\circ\sigma)_i=x_{\sigma(i)}\). Let \(A'\) run _A_ with every call _O<sub>x</sub>_ replaced by \(P_\sigma^{-1}O_xP_\sigma\) and output \(\sigma(I)\). On a fixed order _x_, \(A'\) therefore behaves as _A_ on the order \(x\circ\sigma\), which is uniformly distributed, and the rank of \(\sigma(I)\) under _x_ equals the rank of _I_ under \(x\circ\sigma\). The same \(\sigma\) is used for every call and for the output, so every rank event is uniformized at once. The worst-case success of any algorithm is at most its average success, which gives the second statement.

We average the algorithm over relabelings in Proposition 1, as in the symmetrization of semidefinite programs for ordered search \[27\], whereas Childs and Lee average adversary matrices with the automorphism principle \[34\]. A fresh relabeling between calls would not preserve the oracle answers, and it is not used.

### 3.4 Blind pick and the equivalent blind-pick size

A blind pick selects _s_ designs uniformly at random without comparing them. Its selected set contains a design of the good-enough set with probability

\(B(n,r,s)=1-\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-r}{s}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{s}},\) (3)

the blind-pick alignment probability at alignment level one \[2, 3\]. When a second stage identifies the best of the _s_ designs exactly, as in the two-stage use of OO \[2\], that design is good enough with the same probability. For _r_=1, _B(n,_1_,s_)=_s/n_.

For \(1\le r\le n\) and with \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{a}{b}=\Gamma(a+1)/\big(\Gamma(b+1)\Gamma(a-b+1)\big)\), the ratio in (3) extends to real _s_ in \[0_,n-r_+1\], with _B(n,r,n-r_+1)=1. The logarithmic derivative of the ratio in _s_ is \(\psi(n-r-s+1)-\psi(n-s+1)<0\), where \(\psi\) is the digamma function, so _B(n,r,s_) increases strictly in _s_ from 0 to 1.

**Definition 3.** For \(1\le r\le n\), the equivalent blind-pick size of a value \(P\in[0,1]\) is the unique \(s_\mathrm{eq}(n,r)\in[0,n-r+1]\) with _B(n,r,s_<sub>eq</sub>)=_P_. We write \(s_\mathrm{eq}^Q(n,r)\) for _P=Q<sub>q</sub>(n,r_) and \(s_\mathrm{eq}^C(n,r)\) for _P=C<sub>q</sub>(n,r_). For _r_=1, \(s_\mathrm{eq}^Q(n,1)=nQ_q(n,1)\). We leave the dependence on _P_ and, for the classical and quantum values, on _q_ implicit in this notation.

Using equivalent blind-pick sizes follows the OO practice of comparing selection rules by the selected-set size needed for a given alignment probability \[2\].

### Scope.

Comparisons are exact, meaning noiseless, and the oracle is coherent, so the algorithm may query superpositions of pairs. The budget counts oracle calls. Exact comparisons model problems in which each design is evaluated deterministically but at high cost, such as a unit commitment evaluated against a fixed set of scenarios. Whether such an evaluation can be queried coherently, and at what cost, is the question of Section 8.3. When performance is observed only through noisy simulation, an exact comparison cannot be implemented directly \[9\]. Section 8.2 discusses extensions to that setting.

The choice of cost unit also affects the interpretation. In a model that charges evaluated designs, a blind pick followed by keeping the best is the natural rule. With comparisons as the cost unit, Theorem 1 below shows that _q_ comparisons attain exactly the alignment probability of _q_+1 evaluated designs, although the comparisons can involve up to 2_q_ designs. The results of this paper count comparison queries and make no claim about running time. If a coherent comparison is built from an oracle that evaluates one design, computing and uncomputing both evaluations uses four evaluation calls, and four evaluated designs already contain the best design with probability 4_/n_. The one-comparison gain of Sections 6 and 7 is therefore a gain per comparison and not per evaluation. The order of growth discussed in Section 8.1 does not change under this unit, because _q_ comparisons then cost 4_q_ evaluations while the quantum equivalent blind-pick size grows quadratically in _q_. The gate cost of an oracle call requires a further cost model, as discussed in Section 8.3.

## 4 The classical optimum

The blind-pick formula gives the success probability of a knockout on a random subset with one more design than the comparison budget. We first show that no adaptive comparison<tbc>

procedure can improve this probability with the same budget. This establishes the classical benchmark needed to assess the benefit of coherent access.

**Theorem 1.** _For integers_ \(q\ge 0\), \(n\ge q+1\) _and_ \(0\le r\le n\),

\(C_q(n,r)=1-\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-r}{q+1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{q+1}}=B(n,r,q+1).\) (4)

_The following algorithm attains this value on every order and for every r at once. Choose q_+1 _distinct labels uniformly at random, compare the current winner with the next label q times, and output the final winner. Its output rank law is_

\(Pr[x_I=t]=\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-t}{q}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{q+1}},t\in[n].\) (5)

To prove optimality, we examine the orders consistent with the comparison answers along a branch of an arbitrary comparison tree. The following lemma describes the remaining rank uncertainty in the connected component containing the output label.

**Lemma 1.** _Fix a deterministic comparison tree and a leaf_ \(\ell\) _reached with positive probability under a uniform order. Let_ \(E_\ell\) _be the set of orders that reach_ \(\ell\)_, let a be its output label, and let C be the connected component of a in the graph whose edges are the distinct pairs compared on the path to_ \(\ell\)_. Put k_=|_C|. Conditional on_ \(E_\ell\)_, the set of ranks occupied by C is a uniform k-subset of_ \[_n_\]_, independent of the order within C, and_

\(Pr[x_a=t|E_\ell]=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t-1}{j-1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-t}{k-j}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}},\) (6)

_where_ \(\alpha_j\ge 0\) _is the fraction of linear extensions of the order recorded on C in which a has the j-th smallest rank within C, and_ \(\sum_j\alpha_j=1\).

_Proof._ Each comparison of distinct labels on the path to \(\ell\) records one strict inequality. A self-comparison imposes no constraint. An order reaches \(\ell\) exactly when it satisfies all recorded inequalities, because the tree is deterministic and every answer on the path is prescribed. So \(E_\ell\) is the set of linear extensions of the recorded partial order. Let _D_ be the complement of _C_. No recorded inequality joins _C_ and _D_, and the transitive closure adds none, since a directed path between them would be an undirected path in the comparison graph. Fix a _k_-subset _S_ of ranks and a linear extension \(\pi_C\) of the order on _C_. Place \(\pi_C\) on the ranks _S_ in increasing order. For each linear extension \(\pi_D\) of the order on _D_, place \(\pi_D\) on the complementary ranks. This gives exactly one order in \(E_\ell\) with rank set _S_ on _C_ and internal order \(\pi_C\), and every such order arises once. The count is the number _e<sub>D</sub>_ of linear extensions of the order on _D_, which does not depend on _S_ or \(\pi_C\). The joint law of rank set and internal order is therefore uniform, which proves independence. If _a_ has the _j_-th smallest rank within _C_ under \(\pi_C\), then _x<sub>a</sub>=t_ exactly when _S_ contains _t_, _j_-1 ranks below _t_ and _k-j_ ranks above it, which gives (6).

_Proof of Theorem 1. Attainment._ The output rank is the minimum of a uniform (_q_+1)-subset of ranks. It misses the top _r_ exactly when all _q_+1 ranks exceed _r_, which has probability \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-r}{q+1}/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{q+1}\). The output rank equals _t_ exactly when the subset contains _t_ and _q_ ranks above<tbc>

<tbc>_t_, which gives (5). Because the subset is chosen uniformly, these probabilities hold on every order.

_Upper bound._ By Proposition 1 it suffices to bound the success averaged over a uniform order. Fixing the private randomness turns an algorithm into a deterministic comparison tree with at most _q_ comparisons on every branch, and the average success of the algorithm is the average over seeds of the average success of these trees. Fix a tree and a leaf \(\ell\) of positive probability. Its comparison graph has at most _q_ distinct edges, and a connected graph on _k_ vertices has at least _k_-1 edges, so the component of the output has \(k\le q+1\) vertices. Let _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V_<sub>_q_+1</sub> be a uniformly random sequence of distinct ranks. The set {_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub>_} is a uniform _k_-subset, and for every \(j\le k\) its _j_-th smallest element is at least min(_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub>_), which is at least min(_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V_<sub>_q_+1</sub>). Each term of (6) is the law of the _j_-th smallest element of a uniform _k_-subset, so

\(Pr[x_a\le r|E_\ell]\le Pr[min(V_1,\dots,V_{q+1})\le r]=1-\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-r}{q+1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{q+1}}.\)

Averaging over leaves and seeds gives the bound. Repeated or reversed comparisons add no distinct edge, and a self-comparison adds no edge between distinct labels. Leaves with contradictory answers have probability zero. An output that was never compared has _k_=1 and rank law 1_/n_.

**Corollary 1.** _(i) For_ \(n\ge q+1\) _and_ \(1\le r\le n-q\)_, the equivalent blind-pick size of q exact classical comparisons is exactly_ \(s_\text{eq}^C(n,r)=q+1\)_. (ii) The rank law of every symmetrized classical algorithm with budget q is, on the rank grid, a polynomial in the rank of degree at most_ min(_q,n_-1).

_Proof._ Part (i) is (4), because \(q+1\le n-r+1\) lies in the range where \(B(n,r,\cdot)\) is strictly increasing. For (ii), the symmetrized rank law is the average of (6) over leaves weighted by their probabilities, and each term of (6) has degree \(k-1\le q\) in _t_. Every function on _n_ points is a polynomial of degree at most _n_-1.

Theorem 1 determines the best comparison-based procedure when comparisons are exact and one design is selected. No adaptive choice of pairs improves on a blind pick of _q_+1 designs followed by a knockout, although _q_ comparisons can involve up to 2_q_ designs. Any procedure that returns the best of the same _q_+1 designs with _q_ comparisons attains the same value, whether it compares the current winner with the next design, as in the proof, or plays a bracket. The blind-pick formula itself is classical \[2, 3\], and the winner-rank law of tournament selection without replacement gives the same expression \[35\].

For the upper bound, conditioning on a leaf of a comparison tree with shuffled inputs appears in work on approximate selection with unreliable comparisons \[36\], and lower bounds there and in \[37\] fix the asymptotic order of the number of comparisons. The proof of Theorem 1 is elementary. It uses leaf conditioning, a count of linear extensions and a stochastic comparison of order statistics. The theorem gives the optimum over all adaptive procedures at every budget \(q\le n-1\) and every good-enough set. For \(q\ge n-1\) a knockout of all _n_ designs returns the best one, so _C<sub>q</sub>(n,r_)=1 for every \(r\ge 1\). In the scenario-by-scenario comparison of selection rules proposed in \[2\], Theorem 1 gives the best rule for the scenario of exact comparisons and one selected design. Earlier decision-tree bounds treat randomized<tbc>

<tbc>decision problems \[38\] and verification that a designated element is the maximum \[39\], rather than selection of one design at a fixed budget.

## 5 Rank laws of quantum algorithms

The classical degree bound limits how output probabilities can vary with rank. We now derive the corresponding bound for coherent comparisons and show that it can be attained. The factor two in the degree bound occurs because a probability is quadratic in the amplitudes.

**Theorem 2.** _Let_ \(n\ge 2\) _and let an admissible quantum algorithm use at most q calls to_ (1) _on every branch. After the symmetrization of Proposition 1, its rank law w<sub>t</sub>_=Pr\[_x<sub>I</sub>=t_\], \(t\in[n]\)_, is independent of the order and satisfies w<sub>t</sub>=p(t_) _for a polynomial p of degree at most_ min(2_q,n_-1)_. The degree bound is attained for every q and n._

_Proof._ Write sgn_<sub>ab</sub>(x_)=sgn(_x<sub>a</sub>-x<sub>b</sub>_)=(-1)<sup>**1**</sup><sub>{_x<sub>a</sub>\<x<sub>b</sub>_}</sub> for one orientation of each unordered pair. In the \(|\pm\rangle\) basis of the response bit, each call acts on the address sector (_a,b_) as \(\Pi_++\mathrm{sgn}_{ab}\Pi_-\), on the reversed sector (_b,a_) as \(\Pi_+-\mathrm{sgn}_{ab}\Pi_-\), and on a self-address as the identity. Every unnormalized Kraus trajectory with _k_ calls therefore has amplitudes of degree at most _k_ in the signs, and input-independent operations do not raise the degree. The unconditional probability of each output label is a sum over trajectories, Kraus indices and initial mixtures, so it has degree at most 2_q_. Using \(\mathrm{sgn}_{ab}^2=1\), the probability of output _a_ on order _x_ is

\(p_a(x)=\sum_{E:|E|\le 2q}c_{a,E}\prod_{\{u,v\}\in E}\mathrm{sgn}_{uv}(x),\) (7)

which is the polynomial method \[40\] written in comparison signs.

Regard a monomial in (7) as a graph _G_ with edge set _E_, add the output label _a_ as a vertex, and let the component of _a_ contain _k_ other vertices. Let \(\mu_j\) be the average of the sign product of a detached component _C<sub>j</sub>_ over its internal orders, and let \(\beta_h\) be the average sign product of the root component over the orders of its vertices in which exactly _h_ of the other _k_ vertices have a smaller rank than _a_, with \(\beta_0=1\) when _k_=0. ## 8 Discussion and future work

The results above apply to the instance of QOO with exact comparisons and one selected design. The following questions consider other instances of Definition 1 with larger quantum budgets, comparisons inferred from evaluations and selection of multiple designs. They also address the cost of implementing coherent comparisons and checking feasibility. These changes affect the information available, the success criterion or the cost assigned to a query, so each extension requires a common information and cost model for classical and quantum procedures.

### 8.1 Larger comparison budgets

The two-comparison problem is studied in a companion paper [42], which gives a complete semidefinite characterization of attainable success. Computer-assisted proofs determine the optimum for seven designs and every good-enough set, and for selecting the best of eight designs. In particular, _Q_<sub>2</sub>(7,1)≈0.7166 and _Q_<sub>2</sub>(8,1)≈0.6586. For best-design selection, _nQ_<sub>2</sub>(_n,_1) is nondecreasing and bounded for \(n\ge 7\), with a limit in (7.43710307,7.43815019]. This limit is strictly greater than that of the explicit algorithm family constructed in the companion paper. Two quantum comparisons beat six classical comparisons exactly when \(n\ge 46\). The values for general _n_ and _r_ and the precise scaled limit remain open. Although Theorem 2 restricts the possible rank laws, it does not by itself characterize attainability. The two-comparison characterization resolves this issue at that budget, while explicit reductions and optimal values for higher budgets remain to be determined.

For every budget \(q\ge 1\), the search lower bound [11, 12] gives _nQ<sub>q</sub>(n,_1)=_O(q_<sup>2</sup>) by a reduction. Rank a single marked item first and order the others by label. A comparison of distinct labels _i_ and _j_ is then true exactly when _i_ is marked, or when neither is marked and _i\<j_, which four search queries compute and uncompute. Minimum finding [8] reaches the minimum of a set of designs after an expected number of comparisons of the order of the square root of their number. Stopped at a constant multiple of that expectation, it has found the minimum with probability bounded below by a constant, by Markov’s inequality, so applied to a blind pick of order _q_<sup>2</sup> designs it achieves _nQ<sub>q</sub>(n,_1) of order _q_<sup>2</sup> when _n_ is at least of that order. The exact values and the sharp constants in these bounds are open.

These search bounds are for selecting the best design. For OO, larger budgets should also be studied when the good-enough set remains a fixed fraction of all designs as their number grows. The one-comparison values in Section 7 show that the relative gain in blind-pick units depends on this fraction. Determining that dependence at larger budgets would show when accepting more designs as good enough changes the benefit of quantum comparisons.

### 8.2 Evaluation and selection models

The preceding questions keep comparisons exact. In simulation-based OO, however, comparisons are inferred from observations. Their error probabilities can depend on the performance gaps, so the ordered performance curve affects the alignment probability [3]. Asymptotic query counts for best-arm identification depend on reward gaps [16, 18]. The corresponding question here is the largest alignment probability at a fixed budget, under a specified model of comparison errors.

When comparisons are computed from quantum estimates of design means [43, 44], the budget counts calls to the underlying evaluation oracle. The estimation precision and the<tbc>

<tbc>number of comparisons then have to be chosen together. The problem is to allocate that budget so as to maximize alignment probability, a quantum counterpart of the allocation question addressed by OCBA [14].

An evaluation model can also change what one oracle call answers. A membership query tests whether a single design belongs to the good-enough set instead of comparing two designs. The fixed-budget values of this model can be studied when the number of good designs is unknown [45, 46].

Beyond changes to the evaluation oracle, the output criterion can also change. This paper selects one design and uses alignment level one. Selecting a set with a prescribed alignment level introduces the selected-set size as a further parameter. A fixed-confidence quantum algorithm already identifies a given number of best arms as a set through a reward oracle [19]. The problem for QOO is to determine the best alignment probability under a fixed comparison budget and the corresponding exact classical benchmark.

### 8.3 Computational cost and constrained selection

The evaluation-oracle budget above counts queries rather than total computation. Computational cost also includes the implementation of a coherent comparison, its workspace and the error-correction overhead [47]. The practical question is whether the gain in alignment probability justifies that cost for a specified evaluation model and target probability.

For constrained selection, the cost model also includes feasibility checks. In constrained OO for unit commitment, the selection criterion combines feasibility with sufficiently low cost [4]. The corresponding QOO formulation specifies how feasibility is checked, what information a query returns and how those checks are charged. A performance comparison alone does not supply this information.

Power system screening with deterministic, expensive evaluations on a fixed set of scenarios can provide a first test of this cost model. Classical and quantum procedures would use the same candidates, feasibility rules and target alignment probability. Measuring evaluation, comparison and selection costs would assess the total cost of reaching that target, alongside the alignment probability per query.

## 9 Conclusion

We formulated quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize worst-case alignment probability at a fixed oracle budget. We studied the instance with exact pairwise comparisons, selected-set size one and alignment level one. For exact classical comparisons and a budget smaller than the number of designs, uniform sampling without replacement followed by a knockout is optimal. The sample contains one more design than the budget. With quantum comparisons, the rank law averaged over a random order can have twice the classical degree. We determined the optimum with one comparison from the root of a cubic. These values quantify the benefit of coherent comparison access relative to the optimal classical procedure, and known search bounds show that the quantum-to-classical ratio in blind-pick units grows at most in proportion to the budget for the best design. To determine how that benefit changes beyond the present model, we identify questions about larger budgets, noisy and estimated comparisons, and the computational cost of each comparison as future work.

For a uniform order on _m_ labels the oriented-edge covariance is \((I+D_m^\mathsf{T}D_m)/3\), where _D<sub>m</sub>_ has edge columns _e<sub>i</sub>-e<sub>j</sub>_. The relative order of the other labels is uniform given \(x_1=\ell\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\langle y_w,\phi_x\rangle^2|x_1=\ell]=n/3\). For the cross term, let _Y<sub>j</sub>_ be the relative rank of a label \(j\neq 1\) among the _m_ labels other than 1. This rank is uniform on \[_m_\]. Then \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{sgn}(\ell-x_j)(2Y_j-m-1)]=-2(\ell-1)(m-\ell+1)/m\), and since rank scores and the coordinates of _w_ sum to zero, \(\mathbb{E}[\langle g_w,\phi_x\rangle\langle y_w,\phi_x\rangle|x_1=\ell]=-\sqrt{m}A_\ell/2\). Averaging over \(\ell\le r\) gives \(A_0=n^{-1}\sum_{\ell\le r}A_\ell=2p(r-1)(3n-2r-2)/(3mk)\) and the block \(\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
A_0 & -\sqrt{m}A_0/2 \\
-\sqrt{m}A_0/2 & pn/3
\end{array}\right)\). The rotation \(w\wedge\omega=(-g_w+\sqrt{m}y_w)/\sqrt{n}\), \(b\wedge w=(\sqrt{m}g_w+y_w)/\sqrt{n}\) transforms it into the stated block, with _S=A_<sub>0</sub>+_mp/_3, \(\eta=\sqrt{m}(p/3-A_0/2)\) and \(\tau=p/3\). Exchangeability makes these forms proportional to the inner product on _W_, so orthogonal basis vectors give no cross terms. Writing \(\phi_\mathrm{st}\) and \(\phi_\mathrm{int}\) for the star and internal parts of \(\phi_x\), \(\mathbb{E}[\phi_\mathrm{st}\phi_\mathrm{int}^\mathsf{T}|x_1=\ell]=-(A_\ell/2)D_m\). The internal cycle space \(\Lambda^2W\) has zero incidence, covariance _I/_3, and no coupling to the other blocks, which gives the last block.

## A.3 Upper bound

Let \(Q=p+p\nu\zeta/m\), which is the right side of (10), and define<tbc>

\(\xi=T+\frac{p\nu}{\zeta},\ell_C=\tau+\frac{\eta^2}{\xi-S},\mathcal{L}=QP_0+\xi P_V+\ell_CP_C.\)

<tbc>Then \(\xi-T=p\nu/\zeta>0\) and \(\xi-S=p\nu(3k+2h\zeta)/(3k\zeta)>0\). Also \(\theta/(\xi-T)=\rho\), \(\eta/(\xi-S)=\gamma\) and \(Q-p=(\xi-T)\rho^2\), so the blocks of L-_M_<sub>1</sub> factor as<tbc>

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
Q-p & \theta \\
\theta & \xi-T
\end{array}\right)=(\xi-T)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
\rho \\
1
\end{array}\right)\left(\rho 1
\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\xi-S & -\eta \\
-\eta & \ell_C-\tau
\end{array}\right)=(\xi-S)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
1 \\
-\gamma
\end{array}\right)\left(1-\gamma
\end{array}\right),\)

<tbc>and the last block is \((\xi-S)\gamma^2I\unknown 0\). Hence \(\mathcal{L}\unknown M_1\), and covariance under relabeling gives \(\mathcal{L}\unknown M_i\) for every _i_. Each edge has \(\|P_V(e_i\wedge e_j)\|^2=2/n\) and \(\|P_C(e_i\wedge e_j)\|^2=k/n\), so the edge diagonal of L is \((2\xi+k\ell_C)/n\), and

\(nQ-2\xi-k\ell_C=\frac{p\nu}{m\zeta(3k+2h\zeta)}F_{n,r}(\zeta)=0.\)

Every diagonal entry of L in the feature basis therefore equals _Q_.

To apply this matrix bound to every admissible algorithm, we express its success in the feature coordinates. This is the one-query case of the semidefinite characterization of quantum query algorithms \[31\]. Fix the private randomness of an algorithm, purify it, and absorb the processing after the call into the final measurement. Measurements before the call are input independent and can be deferred. Write the state before the call as \(\sum_{i,j}|i,j\rangle\big(|+\rangle|u_{ij}\rangle+|-\rangle|v_{ij}\rangle\big)+|\chi\rangle\), where \(|\chi\rangle\) is the component of branches that skip the call, flagged in the workspace. In the eigenbasis of the response bit the call fixes the + sector, multiplies the - sector at (_i,j_) with _i\<j_ by sgn(_x<sub>i</sub>-x<sub>j</sub>_), multiplies the reversed pair by the opposite sign, and fixes self-addresses. The state after the call is therefore \(|\Psi_x\rangle=\sum_\mu(\phi_x)_\mu|a_\mu\rangle\), where \((\phi_x)_\mu\) are the coordinates of \(\phi_x\) and<tbc>

\(|a_0\rangle=|\chi\rangle+\sum_{i,j}|i,j,+\rangle|u_{ij}\rangle+\sum_i|i,i,-\rangle|v_{ii}\rangle,|a_{ij}\rangle=|i,j,-\rangle|v_{ij}\rangle-|j,i,-\rangle|v_{ji}\rangle(i<j).\)

<tbc>These vectors have disjoint supports on the flag, address and response registers, so they are orthogonal, and \(\sum_\mu\|a_\mu\|^2=1\). For the output measurement \(\{\widetilde{E}_i\}\) put \((B_i)_{\mu\mu^\prime}=\langle a_\mu|\widetilde{E}_i|a_{\mu^\prime}\rangle\) and \(\lambda_\mu=\|a_\mu\|^2\). Then \(B_i\unknown 0\), \(\sum_iB_i=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda)\) and \(\sum_\mu\lambda_\mu=1\). The matrices _B<sub>i</sub>_ may be complex Hermitian, and since _M<sub>i</sub>_ is real only their real parts contribute to the success. The average success is

\(\sum_i\mathrm{tr}(M_iB_i)\le\sum_i\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}B_i)=\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}\mathrm{diag}(\lambda))=Q.\)

The worst-case success is at most the average, so \(Q_1(n,r)\le Q\).

## A.4 Attainment

The attaining construction uses the kernels of the slack blocks in the upper-bound proof. We give the initial state and measurement, then verify that the measurement is complete and that the success probability equals the bound for every order.

Let \(N=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}=nm/2\), \(\alpha=2mR/(n\zeta^2+2mR)\) and \(\beta=(1-\alpha)/N\). Prepare<tbc>

\(|\psi_\mathrm{in}\rangle=\sqrt{\alpha}|1,1,+\rangle+\sqrt{\beta}\sum_{i<j}|i,j,-\rangle.\)

<tbc>One call gives \(|\psi_x\rangle=C_\alpha\phi_x\) with \(C_\alpha=\sqrt{\alpha}P_0+\sqrt{\beta}(P_V+P_C)\), in the encoding \(|0\rangle=|1,1,+\rangle\) and \(|ij\rangle=|i,j,-\rangle\). In the decomposition (13) define the seed effect

\(E_1=\frac{1}{n}\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & -\sqrt{mR} \\
-\sqrt{mR} & mR
\end{array}\right)\oplus\oplus_{a=1}^k\frac{m}{2n}\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\gamma^2 & \gamma \\
\gamma & 1
\end{array}\right)\oplus 0,\)

and \(E_i=U_\sigma E_1U_\sigma^\mathsf{T}\) for any permutation \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma(1)=i\), where \(U_\sigma\) fixes \(|0\rangle\) and relabels the oriented edges. The seed is invariant under the stabilizer of label 1, so _E<sub>i</sub>_ is well defined. Its traces on the global sectors are 1_/n_, \(mR/n+km\gamma^2/(2n)=m/n\) and _mk/_(2_n_). A label- invariant symmetric matrix on the edge space is a combination of _I_ and \(D_n^\mathsf{T}D_n\), which act as scalars on V and C, and there is no invariant coupling between \(|0\rangle\) and the edges. Since \(\sum_iE_i\) is invariant and its sector traces equal the sector dimensions, \(\sum_iE_i=I\). On the full query space the effects are completed by adding _n_<sup>-1</sup> times the projector onto the complement of the encoded subspace, which the prepared states never reach.

<tbc>Finally \((\alpha/\beta)\rho^2=mR\). The range of the first block of \(C_\alpha E_1C_\alpha\) is the kernel of the first slack block, spanned by \((1,-\rho)^\mathsf{T}\). The range of each repeated block is the kernel of the second slack block, spanned by \((\gamma,1)^\mathsf{T}\). So \(\mathrm{tr}[(\mathcal{L}-M_1)C_\alpha E_1C_\alpha]=0\), and by covariance the same holds for every _i_. The average success is

\(\sum_i\mathrm{tr}(M_iC_\alpha E_iC_\alpha)=\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}C_\alpha^2)=\alpha Q+N\beta Q=Q,\)

and covariance of the state family makes the success equal to _Q_ on every order.

The closed forms in Corollary 2 follow from the same cubic. For _r_=1, _F_<sub>_n,_1</sub>(_z_)=2_k(z_+1)\[_nz_<sup>2</sup>+(3-_n)z_-3_m_\], whose positive root \((n-3+\sqrt{13n^2-18n+9})/(2n)\) gives the first closed form. For _r=n/_2, _h_=0 gives the second closed form.
